transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, I'm here because my body just feels completely drained. It's... well, it takes everything I have right now just to do the basics. Like, even just walking from my car into the clinic today, or being at work and just trying to open the EHR... it just takes everything out of me. I'm just completely exhausted.
How long have you been feeling this exhausted—days, weeks, or months?

It's been months. Um, about nine months, I'd say. This whole exhausted, depressed... and just guilty feeling has been going on since I crashed. Before that, I had this period where I just had a ton of energy, but ever since that ended, it's been exactly nine months of feeling like this.

Tell me more about that period before you 'crashed' when you had a ton of energy—how long did it last, and did you notice things like needing much less sleep, feeling unusually confident or irritable, or racing thoughts during that time?

Um, I'm not really sure about the exact amount of time it lasted, or... or the racing thoughts and all that. But I do remember I had so much energy during that time that I literally couldn't sit still. 

Like at work, I would just keep walking the halls, reorganizing all the supplies, checking the rooms over and over... I was just constantly looking for more things to do, even after my shift should have been over. I just couldn't stop moving and doing things back then.
Thinking back, roughly how many days in a row did that period of high energy and constant activity last?

Um, I honestly don't know. It's hard to remember exactly how many days it was. It all just kind of blends together when I try to think back on it now. I just remember not being able to stop moving, but... yeah, I really couldn't tell you an exact number of days.
During that period when you had all that extra energy, did you notice you needed much less sleep than usual—like only sleeping a few hours a night but still feeling fine?

Yeah, back then... I could sleep for just two or three hours and still feel completely wired. It was like I didn't even need it. But lately, it's been the exact opposite. Now I either wake up way before dawn just feeling sick with worry, or I end up sleeping half the day and still feel completely exhausted anyway.
During that time when you had all that extra energy, did coworkers, friends, or family notice a change in you, or did it cause any problems at work or in your relationships?

Yeah, people definitely noticed. It actually caused a lot of problems at work. Um, I got to the point where I couldn't finish my documentation safely, and I couldn't stay focused on any of my patient-support tasks. It was bad enough that employee health actually pulled me from work and sent me for an emergency evaluation. 

And outside of work, it messed things up too. I was supposed to be preparing for my CNA certification, but I had to stop doing that seriously because I just couldn't keep up with it. So, yeah, it definitely affected a lot of things.

During this depressive period, have you experienced any unusual perceptions—like hearing voices or seeing things others don't—or strong beliefs that others might find hard to believe, such as feeling you're being watched or punished?

No, not right now while I'm feeling like this. Um, the stuff like that... like having this idea that I was on a special medical mission, or hearing my name and the medical monitors calling out to me... that really only happened back when I was totally wired and barely sleeping, trying to overhaul the whole clinic. 

Once that high-energy period ended, all that stopped. I'm definitely not hearing those things or feeling chosen anymore.
Have you noticed feeling unusually cold, or having dry skin and hair thinning, over these past several months?
No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I don't think I've been feeling colder than usual, and my skin and hair seem pretty much the same as they always are.
Has anyone told you that you snore loudly, gasp, or seem to stop breathing for moments while you're asleep?

No, nobody's ever mentioned anything like that to me. I mean, I sleep alone, but even when I've been around others or, you know, falling asleep on the couch with family around, no one has ever said I snore loudly or stop breathing or anything.
During these past nine months of feeling this way, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or that you'd be better off not being here?

No, I haven't. I mean, I feel really down, and everything just feels heavy and pointless right now, but... no, I haven't had any thoughts about hurting myself or wanting to die. I just want to feel normal again.
Right now, how is this depression affecting your ability to go to work, take care of yourself, or manage your daily responsibilities?

It's pretty bad. I mean, it got to the point where I couldn't even finish my documentation safely at work. I couldn't stay focused on supporting the patients, so... employee health actually pulled me from my shifts and sent me for an emergency evaluation. And I was trying to prepare for my CNA certification, but I had to stop doing that too because I just couldn't keep up with the studying or anything else.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's chief complaint and reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a clear past manic episode (markedly elevated energy, decreased need for sleep to 2-3 hours with no fatigue, psychomotor agitation, grandiose/psychotic ideas about a 'medical mission' and hearing her name called by monitors, and severe functional impairment requiring emergency evaluation and work removal), followed by a current major depressive episode lasting ~9 months with depressed mood, guilt, anhedonia, fatigue, sleep disturbance (early morning waking and hypersomnia), and significant functional impairment (unable to work, unable to pursue CNA certification). No psychotic symptoms, hallucinations, or delusions are present during the current depressive episode, and no suicidal ideation is endorsed. This pattern—Bipolar I Disorder with a documented prior manic episode with psychotic features, now presenting with a current severe depressive episode without psychotic features—is diagnostic of F31.4. F31.5 was considered but ruled out due to absence of current psychotic features. F33.2 (recurrent MDD, severe) was considered but excluded given clear historical evidence of a manic episode with psychotic features, confirming bipolar rather than unipolar depression.

confirmed_symptoms: Markedly increased energy and inability to sit still
Decreased need for sleep (2-3 hours, felt wired/no fatigue)
Excessive goal-directed activity (reorganizing supplies, checking rooms repeatedly)
Grandiose delusion (belief she was on a 'special medical mission')
Auditory hallucinations (hearing her name and medical monitors calling her)
Severe impairment requiring removal from work and emergency evaluation
Impaired ability to complete CNA certification studies
Pervasive fatigue and low energy affecting basic tasks
Sleep disturbance (early morning waking with anxiety, or hypersomnia)
Significant functional impairment (unable to safely complete work documentation, unable to focus on patient care tasks)

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Current depressive episode has persisted for approximately 9 months since the manic episode ended; duration of prior manic episode not precisely recalled by patient but associated with significant functional disruption.
additional_requirements: History of a distinct manic episode with psychotic features confirmed (grandiosity, auditory hallucinations, decreased sleep, hyperactivity)
Current episode is depressive in nature without psychotic features
Medical/organic causes for fatigue (hypothyroidism, sleep apnea) screened and ruled out by patient report
